analysis.one_liner: Requires the President and Vice President to disclose and divest financial conflicts, including releasing tax returns.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced days before a new president took office, was referred to a Senate committee and never received a vote; it died when the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the President and Vice President to disclose their families' financial interests to Congress and the Office of Government Ethics, release three years of tax returns, and move any holdings that could conflict with their official duties into a blind trust that sells them off. It would bar presidential appointees from working on matters involving the President's or the First Family's finances, extend the ban on government contracts to the President and Vice President, and require major-party presidential nominees to release tax returns. It also lets the Attorney General, state attorneys general, or ordinary citizens go to court to enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would gain visibility into whether the nation's top two officials are making decisions that enrich themselves or their families. Government employees would gain clearer rules about steering decisions away from the President's private holdings.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the President and Vice President to file a detailed disclosure of financial interests of themselves, their spouses, and minor children within 30 days of taking office, and includes three years of tax returns in the disclosure [S2] [S3].

Requires divestiture of any financial interest posing a potential conflict of interest by transferring it to a qualified blind trust, whose trustee must sell it and reinvest the proceeds in conflict-free holdings [S2] [S3].

Requires major-party presidential nominees and sitting Presidents to make their last three years of income tax returns publicly available, with the Office of Government Ethics or the Federal Election Commission empowered to obtain them from the Treasury if not voluntarily disclosed [S2] [S3].

Requires presidential appointees to recuse themselves from any matter involving the President or the President's spouse and their substantial financial interests, with career staff stepping in [S2] [S3].

Extends the existing ban on Members of Congress entering federal contracts to the President and Vice President, and gives the Attorney General, state attorneys general, and aggrieved persons standing to seek court orders enforcing the divestiture rules [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The President, Vice President, and their families, who would have to disclose their finances, publish tax returns, and sell off holdings that overlap with their official duties. Major-party presidential nominees would also have to release tax returns.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sitting presidents, vice presidents, and their families

drawbacks.text: The enforcement provision allows any 'aggrieved person' or any state attorney general to sue the President over divestiture, which could invite politically motivated litigation against whoever holds the office, not just in the moment it was written [S3].

Forcing a sitting president to sell business assets on a court-enforced timeline raises unresolved constitutional questions about how far Congress can regulate the presidency, which the bill itself acknowledges by including a rule of construction and a severability clause [S3].

Declaring by 'sense of Congress' that a violation would be a high crime or misdemeanor is symbolic; the Constitution vests impeachment in the House and Senate, so the declaration adds no enforceable penalty [S2] [S3].
Mandatory public release of tax returns reduces financial privacy for the officeholder and their family, a cost an honest supporter of transparency would acknowledge [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real gap: sitting presidents and vice presidents are not covered by the conflict-of-interest rules that bind other federal officials, so financial conflicts at the top of the executive branch had no legal remedy. The main costs are constitutional uncertainty around forcing divestiture and the risk of nuisance lawsuits under the broad enforcement clause. On balance it is a serious attempt to close an enforcement gap, though its most sweeping provisions would likely have faced court challenges.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill and sent it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on January 9, 2017, eleven days before the presidential inauguration, with an initial group of 24 Democratic cosponsors [S3] [S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs on the day of introduction [S1] [S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill; it received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote during the 115th Congress [S5].
The bill attracted 32 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, and it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting officeholders and their family business interests were better off, since no disclosure, divestiture, or tax-return requirement was ever enacted. Presidential nominees likewise remained free to withhold tax returns.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of the Senate's Republicans signed on.

against.what_they_did: No Senate Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-led committee and Senate never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 senators behind the bill were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored it, and the Republican-controlled committee never took it up.

industries.industry: Family business holdings of sitting presidents and their families
industries.note: The bill would have forced divestiture of any interest posing a potential conflict of interest, including payments from foreign governments, and subjected the president's family businesses to annual ethics review and possible lawsuits. Its defeat meant those holdings faced no new legal requirements.

Nominees would have had to publish three years of tax returns within 15 days of nomination, with the FEC able to obtain them from the Treasury otherwise. Without the law, nominees could decline to release returns.
